title: The general of the dhamma
hook: Sariputta, foremost in wisdom, who could explain what the Buddha said briefly

segments.voice: Yesterday, deathless, and your line: he ran to tell him. What did you hand to someone before it cooled? Today, the friend who ran becomes the one who explains. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

A brahmin named Sela has just met the Buddha, and he is won over. He is also a practical man. A teacher this great, he reasons, must have someone at his side who carries the work forward, the way a king has a general. So, in the Sutta Nipata, Sela asks it in verse: who is your general? Which disciple follows the teacher and keeps this going? It's a fair question about any movement. Somebody has to explain the thing on the days the founder isn't in the room. The Buddha answers with one name.
screen: `SELA IS WON OVER.` → `WHO IS YOUR GENERAL?` → `ONE NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the name: Sariputta. In paraphrase, the Buddha tells Sela: the wheel of the teaching that I set rolling, Sariputta keeps rolling, the one who comes after me. That's where the picture of a general comes from. Not a battle. A wheel that needs someone to keep it moving. Later tradition turned it into a title: the general of the dhamma. Second, what he was known for. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of disciples who were foremost in one quality or another, the Buddha names Sariputta foremost in great wisdom. And in the discourses his wisdom has a recognizable shape: the Buddha says something short, and Sariputta opens it up so others can use it. Third, one scene of that. In the Samyutta Nikaya, a group of monks is about to leave for a far western country. The Buddha tells them: before you go, take leave of Sariputta. He's wise, and he helps his fellow monks. So they go to him, and he gets them ready. Out there, he says, wise people will question you. They'll ask what your teacher teaches. Answer simply: the removal of desire and lust. And if they ask, desire for what? Tell them: for the body, for feelings, for perceptions, for the rest of what we take ourselves to be. One plain line first, then the next step only if someone asks for it. That is the general at work: not commanding, but equipping. Looking back over this week, from the end of the poem to the start of the disciples: Ashvaghosha himself, honey, the poem closed, Upatissa, a pact, deathless, and today, the one who explains.
screen: `WHO KEEPS THE WHEEL ROLLING?` · `FOREMOST IN GREAT WISDOM.` · `GETTING TRAVELERS READY.` · `ONE PLAIN LINE FIRST.` · then, large: `WISDOM EXPLAINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain one thing clearly. Settle, and breathe. Choose something you understand well. How to make rice. Why your team uses a certain tool. What a word in this path means. Now, silently, explain it the way Sariputta coached the travelers: one plain sentence first. Stop there. Imagine someone asking, what do you mean? Give the next sentence. Then stop again. If you notice yourself reaching for a long speech, come back to the breath, and to one plain sentence. The bell holds the time.
Sariputta. The disciple the Buddha named, when Sela asked who kept the wheel of the teaching rolling, foremost in wisdom, who readied others to explain it simply.
Your line: wisdom explains. Today, when someone asks you something, give one plain sentence, then wait to see if they want the next. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: In Theravada communities Sariputta is honored as the chief disciple in wisdom, and his discourses in the Pali texts are studied as models of how to explain the teaching step by step.

original.note: Pali: general (senapati) of the dhamma, a title later tradition gives Sariputta.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sariputta was some kind of commander.
what it means: the Buddha sets the wheel of teaching rolling, and Sariputta keeps it moving by explaining it.
what a scholar hears: in the Sutta Nipata, Sela asks 'who is your general?' and the Buddha answers with Sariputta's name; later tradition makes it a title.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 3.7, Sela Sutta (verses 556–557; also Majjhima Nikaya 92)
Anguttara Nikaya 1.188 (Etadagga Vagga: foremost in great wisdom)

notes: All material paraphrased. Confirm Sn 556–557: Sela asks who is the general (senapati) who follows the teacher and keeps the wheel turning; the Buddha answers that Sariputta, born after the Tathagata, keeps turning the wheel he set rolling.
Confirm the exact AN 1 sutta number for Sariputta as foremost in great wisdom (numbering varies by edition).

SN 22.2: confirm the monks were bound for the western country, the Buddha's description of Sariputta as wise and a helper of his fellow monks, and the answer sequence (removal of desire and lust for form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness). The script lists 'body, feelings, perceptions, the rest' as a plain-language summary of the five aggregates.
'Dhammasenapati' as a title is from the commentarial tradition; the script attributes it to 'later tradition'.
Week-end look back (days 722–728) is the last lines of the teach.
Editor: added 'First' to the teach's first step, softened 'again and again' to a plain description, and smoothed the garbled week look-back sentence.
